BACKGROUND: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is a key component of global 
cervical cancer elimination strategies. While substantial declines in cervical 
cancer incidence have been observed in several countries, evidence of its effect 
on mortality is scarce. England introduced a national HPV vaccination programme 
in 2008 for girls aged 12-13 years (achieving 80-90% coverage before the 
COVID-19 pandemic), with a catch-up campaign in 2008-10 for girls aged 14-18 
years. We aimed to investigate trends in cervical cancer mortality and to 
estimate the reduction in cervical cancer deaths in young women in England 
following the introduction of HPV vaccination.
METHODS: We analysed population-based cervical cancer mortality data from 
England between 2001 and 2024 among women aged 20-24, 25-29, and 30-34 years. 
HPV vaccination coverage by birth cohort was obtained from official reports and 
used to estimate, for each age group and calendar year of death, the proportion 
of women who had been vaccinated. We plotted observed and adjusted age-specific 
mortality rates against year of death and overlaid a smoothed curve. Poisson 
regression applied to the numbers of deaths was used to estimate the relative 
risk reduction in vaccinated women compared with what was expected in the 
absence of vaccination, assuming no herd immunity. Confidence intervals were 
obtained by inverting the likelihood ratio test.
FINDINGS: In women aged 20-24 years between 2020 and 2024, in whom vaccination 
coverage was around 88-90% at age 12-13 years, no deaths occurred, compared with 
23·1 expected deaths based on historical rates, corresponding to a mortality 
reduction of 100% (95% CI 84-100). In earlier birth cohorts, who were offered 
vaccination up to age 18 years with coverage of around 63-87%, mortality 
reductions of 80% (51-94) in women aged 20-24 years in 2015-19, and 69% (55-79) 
in women aged 25-29 years in 2020-24 were observed. The relative risk reduction

To ensure comparability of genital HPV prevalence between POP-Brazil 1 and POP-Brazil 2, prevalence was estimated based on positive cases for the 26 genotypes detected by both the Linear Array® Genotyping Test (used in POP1) and the Anyplex™ II HPV28 Detection (used in POP2): 6, 11, 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 40, 42, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 56, 58, 59, 61, 66, 68, 69, 70, 73, and 82. Results were categorized as: (i) overall HPV (positive for any genital HPV); (ii) multiple infection (more than one genital HPV type detected); (iii) high-risk HPV (positive for any genital high-risk HPV type: 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, and 68), whose definition was based on the test classification derived from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, according to study protocol; (iv) high-risk genital HPV except 16 and 18; (v) 4vHPV (HPV types included in the quadrivalent vaccine: 6, 11, 16, 18); and (vi) 9vHPV (types in the nonavalent vaccine: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). Results were considered negative when none of the 26 overlapping HPV genotypes were detected. Invalid (missing) samples due to insufficient genetic material for analysis were excluded (Fig. 1).

## Abstract

Human papillomavirus vaccination is central to cervical cancer elimination, yet population-level evidence from middle-income countries remains limited. We evaluated the impact of quadrivalent HPV vaccination in Brazil using data from two repeated population-based cross-sectional surveys conducted in 2016–2017 and 2020–2023 among sexually active individuals aged 16–25 years. Genital samples were tested for HPV genotyping and survey-weighted Poisson-regression models adjusted for sociodemographic and behavioral factors were used to compare prevalences between periods. Among 11,794 women and 4932 men, the prevalence of vaccine-type HPV declined from 15.64% (14.23–17.17) to 5.92% (5.23–6.70) among women and 13.81% (11.15–16.99) to 10.39% (8.35–12.85) among men. Adjusted analyses showed an 81% reduction among vaccinated women (PR0.19; 0.14–0.27) and a 33% reduction among unvaccinated women (PR0.67; 0.55–0.81), suggesting both direct and indirect effects. Reductions were significant only among women aged 16–23, the group with higher coverage. Among men, lower prevalence of vaccine-type HPV was observed only among vaccinated individuals (PR0.39; 0.18–0.86). The overall HPV prevalence increased modestly between the two surveys. No differences in prevalence reduction were observed according to the number of vaccine doses. These findings demonstrated the impact of HPV vaccination in Brazil and highlight the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage and continued surveillance.

The decrease in prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine was higher in women than in men, particularly among individuals younger than 21 years. Differences in HPV vaccination uptake opportunities should be considered when interpreting vaccine impact and coverage by age group and sex. Most older participants ( ≥ 21 years) had already exceeded the initial target age at vaccine introduction in 2014 and were therefore less likely to have been vaccinated. This was particularly true for boys, who were only included in the program from 2017 onward<sup>6</sup>. As a result, reductions in HPV prevalence among men in general are expected to rely largely on indirect protection conferred by high vaccination coverage in women, which may explain the less pronounced decrease observed in men in POP2. This finding is not unexpected, as boys typically receive less routine support for HPV vaccination than girls, partly because HPV is still widely perceived primarily as a cause of cervical cancer. Consequently, most studies evaluating the impact of HPV vaccination have focused exclusively on girls. Among the 164 countries with HPV vaccination programs monitored by the WHO, only 85 (51.8%) have expanded vaccination for boys until 2026<sup>28</sup>. A systematic review showed that gender-neutral HPV vaccination is a cost-effective strategy, although its cost-effectiveness is highly dependent on vaccination coverage<sup>29</sup>.

There was no difference in the prevalence of 4vHPV types according to the number of vaccine doses received, suggesting that a single-dose HPV vaccination regime may be sufficient to confer protection, in line with current WHO recommendations<sup>1</sup>. Consistent with these findings, a recent systematic review found no evidence of differences in HPV16 and HPV18 detection across different dose schedules among vaccinated individuals<sup>30</sup>.

In Brazil, the quadrivalent vaccine was introduced in the public immunization program as a two-dose schedule in 2014, initially targeting girls aged 11–13 years. A year later, the program was expanded to include younger girls, lowering the minimum age to nine years. In 2017, it was further extended to older girls, raising the maximum age to 14 years and also including boys (aged 11–14 years) and high-risk adult populations, such as people living with HIV, oncology patients, and those who had undergone solid organ or bone marrow transplants<sup>6</sup>. Since 2024, the vaccination schedule has been updated to a single dose for boys and girls aged 9–14 years, and for the catch-up of unvaccinated adolescents of both sexes aged 15–19 years in 2025. The HPV vaccination was also expanded to pre-exposure prophylaxis users, victims of sexual violence, individuals with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis<sup>6</sup>. Considering the first dose, the vaccination coverage in Brazil was estimated at 83.21% among women and 67.57% among men aged 9–14 years in 2024<sup>7</sup>.

Just three years after the vaccine’s introduction in Brazil, our previous findings showed that vaccinated girls had significantly lower prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to unvaccinated ones<sup>8</sup>. However, a decade after the implementation of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Brazil, the real population-level impact on HPV prevalence remains largely unknown when comparing pre- and post-vaccine eras. While several studies have demonstrated positive vaccine impact in HPV prevalence, they primarily focus on high-income countries, with limited data from Latin America, a region with extensive vaccination programs and high cervical cancer incidence<sup>9,10</sup>. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the population-level impact of HPV vaccination on HPV prevalence among Brazilians aged 16–25.

### Sample collection

Sample collection followed the study protocol<sup>32</sup>. Cervical samples were collected by a health professional, while penile samples were obtained through supervised self-collection using one sterile swab scrubbed across the penile shaft, glans penis, and coronal sulcus. Samples were stored at controlled room temperature (15-25 °C) and shipped to the laboratory of clinical epidemiology at the Federal University of Health Sciences of Porto Alegre (EpiClin-UFCSPA), where they were aliquoted and kept at -80 °C until use.

## Introduction

Vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) is one of the key prevention strategies to reduce HPV-associated cancers and achieve the World Health Organization (WHO) goals of cervical cancer elimination until 2030<sup>1,2</sup>. The quadrivalent HPV (4vHPV) vaccine, which protects against genotypes 6, 11, 16, and 18 (responsible for most genital warts and 80–90% of HPV-related cancers), has been incorporated into several national vaccination programs, pioneered by countries such as Australia, Mexico, and the United States as early as 2006<sup>2</sup>.

Many real-world studies have demonstrated the vaccination impact through significant reductions in the prevalence of high-risk HPV in high-income countries. For instance, the prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine decreased from 11.5 to 3.3% when comparing the pre- and post-vaccine eras in the USA<sup>3</sup>. In Australia, among 18- to 24-year-old women, it dropped from 28.7 to 6.7%<sup>4</sup>. Moreover, the prevalence of oncogenic genital HPV infections (types 16 and 18) decreased significantly among girls and women after vaccine implementation, with greater reductions observed at younger ages, as shown by a meta-analysis with data from 14 high-income countries<sup>5</sup>.

These findings are consistent with results from HPV vaccination programs throughout the Americas, spanning high-, middle-, and low-income countries. In high-income countries, vaccine impact ranged from 74 to 93% in adolescents aged 9–14 years and 12–90% in those aged 15–18<sup>11</sup>. A meta-analysis from high-income countries similarly demonstrated higher reductions among younger girls, with HPV 16 and 18 prevalence decreasing by 83% among those aged 13–19 compared to 66% among women aged 20–24 years, after 5–8 years of vaccine implementation<sup>5</sup>. In Colombia, data from individuals in the same age range show a reduction in HPV 16 and 18 from 15.4 to 6.5%, with higher impact for vaccination occurring before sexual debut<sup>12</sup>. Similarly, vaccination decreased the prevalence of overall and quadrivalent-specific HPV types among girls recruited in public hospitals in Argentina<sup>13</sup>. In the United States, data from New Mexico show a 75–80% relative reduction in prevalence of HPV genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine among screened women, while the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) demonstrates an even greater decrease, from 18.5% pre-vaccination to 2.8% after vaccine implementation<sup>3,14</sup>. Beyond demonstrating clinical impact, evidence from a systematic review indicates that vaccinating girls against HPV is a cost-effective strategy for Latin American countries<sup>15</sup>.

## Abstract

Human papillomavirus vaccination is central to cervical cancer elimination, yet population-level evidence from middle-income countries remains limited. We evaluated the impact of quadrivalent HPV vaccination in Brazil using data from two repeated population-based cross-sectional surveys conducted in 2016–2017 and 2020–2023 among sexually active individuals aged 16–25 years. Genital samples were tested for HPV genotyping and survey-weighted Poisson-regression models adjusted for sociodemographic and behavioral factors were used to compare prevalences between periods. Among 11,794 women and 4932 men, the prevalence of vaccine-type HPV declined from 15.64% (14.23–17.17) to 5.92% (5.23–6.70) among women and 13.81% (11.15–16.99) to 10.39% (8.35–12.85) among men. Adjusted analyses showed an 81% reduction among vaccinated women (PR0.19; 0.14–0.27) and a 33% reduction among unvaccinated women (PR0.67; 0.55–0.81), suggesting both direct and indirect effects. Reductions were significant only among women aged 16–23, the group with higher coverage. Among men, lower prevalence of vaccine-type HPV was observed only among vaccinated individuals (PR0.39; 0.18–0.86). The overall HPV prevalence increased modestly between the two surveys. No differences in prevalence reduction were observed according to the number of vaccine doses. These findings demonstrated the impact of HPV vaccination in Brazil and highlight the importance of maintaining high vaccination coverage and continued surveillance.

The decrease in prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine was higher in women than in men, particularly among individuals younger than 21 years. Differences in HPV vaccination uptake opportunities should be considered when interpreting vaccine impact and coverage by age group and sex. Most older participants ( ≥ 21 years) had already exceeded the initial target age at vaccine introduction in 2014 and were therefore less likely to have been vaccinated. This was particularly true for boys, who were only included in the program from 2017 onward<sup>6</sup>. As a result, reductions in HPV prevalence among men in general are expected to rely largely on indirect protection conferred by high vaccination coverage in women, which may explain the less pronounced decrease observed in men in POP2. This finding is not unexpected, as boys typically receive less routine support for HPV vaccination than girls, partly because HPV is still widely perceived primarily as a cause of cervical cancer. Consequently, most studies evaluating the impact of HPV vaccination have focused exclusively on girls. Among the 164 countries with HPV vaccination programs monitored by the WHO, only 85 (51.8%) have expanded vaccination for boys until 2026<sup>28</sup>. A systematic review showed that gender-neutral HPV vaccination is a cost-effective strategy, although its cost-effectiveness is highly dependent on vaccination coverage<sup>29</sup>.

There was no difference in the prevalence of 4vHPV types according to the number of vaccine doses received, suggesting that a single-dose HPV vaccination regime may be sufficient to confer protection, in line with current WHO recommendations<sup>1</sup>. Consistent with these findings, a recent systematic review found no evidence of differences in HPV16 and HPV18 detection across different dose schedules among vaccinated individuals<sup>30</sup>.

In Brazil, the quadrivalent vaccine was introduced in the public immunization program as a two-dose schedule in 2014, initially targeting girls aged 11–13 years. A year later, the program was expanded to include younger girls, lowering the minimum age to nine years. In 2017, it was further extended to older girls, raising the maximum age to 14 years and also including boys (aged 11–14 years) and high-risk adult populations, such as people living with HIV, oncology patients, and those who had undergone solid organ or bone marrow transplants<sup>6</sup>. Since 2024, the vaccination schedule has been updated to a single dose for boys and girls aged 9–14 years, and for the catch-up of unvaccinated adolescents of both sexes aged 15–19 years in 2025. The HPV vaccination was also expanded to pre-exposure prophylaxis users, victims of sexual violence, individuals with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis<sup>6</sup>. Considering the first dose, the vaccination coverage in Brazil was estimated at 83.21% among women and 67.57% among men aged 9–14 years in 2024<sup>7</sup>.

Just three years after the vaccine’s introduction in Brazil, our previous findings showed that vaccinated girls had significantly lower prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine compared to unvaccinated ones<sup>8</sup>. However, a decade after the implementation of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine in Brazil, the real population-level impact on HPV prevalence remains largely unknown when comparing pre- and post-vaccine eras. While several studies have demonstrated positive vaccine impact in HPV prevalence, they primarily focus on high-income countries, with limited data from Latin America, a region with extensive vaccination programs and high cervical cancer incidence<sup>9,10</sup>. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate the population-level impact of HPV vaccination on HPV prevalence among Brazilians aged 16–25.

### Sample collection

Sample collection followed the study protocol<sup>32</sup>. Cervical samples were collected by a health professional, while penile samples were obtained through supervised self-collection using one sterile swab scrubbed across the penile shaft, glans penis, and coronal sulcus. Samples were stored at controlled room temperature (15-25 °C) and shipped to the laboratory of clinical epidemiology at the Federal University of Health Sciences of Porto Alegre (EpiClin-UFCSPA), where they were aliquoted and kept at -80 °C until use.

## Introduction

Vaccination against human papillomavirus (HPV) is one of the key prevention strategies to reduce HPV-associated cancers and achieve the World Health Organization (WHO) goals of cervical cancer elimination until 2030<sup>1,2</sup>. The quadrivalent HPV (4vHPV) vaccine, which protects against genotypes 6, 11, 16, and 18 (responsible for most genital warts and 80–90% of HPV-related cancers), has been incorporated into several national vaccination programs, pioneered by countries such as Australia, Mexico, and the United States as early as 2006<sup>2</sup>.

Many real-world studies have demonstrated the vaccination impact through significant reductions in the prevalence of high-risk HPV in high-income countries. For instance, the prevalence of genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine decreased from 11.5 to 3.3% when comparing the pre- and post-vaccine eras in the USA<sup>3</sup>. In Australia, among 18- to 24-year-old women, it dropped from 28.7 to 6.7%<sup>4</sup>. Moreover, the prevalence of oncogenic genital HPV infections (types 16 and 18) decreased significantly among girls and women after vaccine implementation, with greater reductions observed at younger ages, as shown by a meta-analysis with data from 14 high-income countries<sup>5</sup>.

These findings are consistent with results from HPV vaccination programs throughout the Americas, spanning high-, middle-, and low-income countries. In high-income countries, vaccine impact ranged from 74 to 93% in adolescents aged 9–14 years and 12–90% in those aged 15–18<sup>11</sup>. A meta-analysis from high-income countries similarly demonstrated higher reductions among younger girls, with HPV 16 and 18 prevalence decreasing by 83% among those aged 13–19 compared to 66% among women aged 20–24 years, after 5–8 years of vaccine implementation<sup>5</sup>. In Colombia, data from individuals in the same age range show a reduction in HPV 16 and 18 from 15.4 to 6.5%, with higher impact for vaccination occurring before sexual debut<sup>12</sup>. Similarly, vaccination decreased the prevalence of overall and quadrivalent-specific HPV types among girls recruited in public hospitals in Argentina<sup>13</sup>. In the United States, data from New Mexico show a 75–80% relative reduction in prevalence of HPV genotypes covered by the 4vHPV vaccine among screened women, while the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) demonstrates an even greater decrease, from 18.5% pre-vaccination to 2.8% after vaccine implementation<sup>3,14</sup>. Beyond demonstrating clinical impact, evidence from a systematic review indicates that vaccinating girls against HPV is a cost-effective strategy for Latin American countries<sup>15</sup>.
